choices: Fault domains — spread instances across the 3 fault domains inside one AD to survive a rack-level failure, and availability domains to survive an AD-level failure
Compartments — isolate workloads with policies so a power event cannot cross a policy boundary
VCN route tables — route database traffic to a backup table when the primary fails
Object Storage buckets — replicate data across buckets, which are isolated power zones
scenarios.hint: OCI has two levels of isolation: one is a set of fault domains sharing a datacenter, the other is an independent datacenter entirely.
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI construct maps to 'different power/cooling/network' isolation, and how would you use it?
scenarios.situation: A startup runs its database primary on one rack and the replica on another rack in the same building. A power bus failure takes down the whole building. The CTO says: 'In OCI, how would we have isolated the two failures — hardware and power?'
scenarios.title: The two-failure scenario
scenarios.why: An availability domain is one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling, and networking — an AD-level failure is contained. Within an AD, three fault domains group racks on different hardware, so a rack failure affects only one fault domain. The pattern: replicate across ADs for site resilience, and across fault domains inside an AD for hardware resilience.

choices: Fault domains protect against rack-level failure inside one AD, but not a full region outage — cross-region replication or a multi-AD region is needed for regional DR
Fault domains require 3 ADs to function; with one AD they silently do nothing
A single-AD region cannot run compute instances, only storage
Multi-AD HA is impossible in OCI; every design must be single-AD
scenarios.hint: Ask: what is the blast radius of a fault domain versus a region?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this design?
scenarios.situation: A team wants multi-AD high availability for their order system. They pick a region that has only one availability domain and deploy 'primary in fault domain 1, standby in fault domain 2'. Their DR test then kills the whole region.
scenarios.title: The single-AD region bet
scenarios.why: Fault domains are intra-AD resilience (independent racks, shared datacenter infrastructure), while regions are independent geographies. Some OCI regions have 1 AD and some have 3. Surviving a region-level event requires a second region (e.g., async replication to a paired region), not more fault domains. Match the failure scope to the isolation construct.

choices: Dedicated Region — a full OCI region operated by Oracle inside the customer's own datacenter, meeting residency and on-premises requirements
A second public region — data residency is satisfied by any EU region
Object Storage Archive tier — archived data is exempt from residency law
IAM compartments — policies can pin data to a country
scenarios.hint: Which OCI option literally puts an entire region inside the customer's building?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI deployment option fits?
scenarios.situation: A European bank must keep customer data inside its own country and needs cloud services behind its firewall for low-latency trading. Public OCI regions don't satisfy legal.
scenarios.title: The data-residency request
scenarios.why: OCI's distributed cloud includes Dedicated Region (a complete OCI region in the customer's datacenter), Oracle Alloy (partners run their own cloud), and Roving Edge for disconnected edge sites. Dedicated Region is the answer for strict residency plus cloud services on-premises; a public region in the same country may satisfy residency but not the behind-the-firewall requirement.

choices: The home region cannot be changed after tenancy creation — IAM resources live in the home region; subscribe to additional regions for workloads instead
The home region can be moved once per year via a support ticket
Changing the home region is automatic when the billing address changes
The home region follows the first VCN created, not the tenancy
scenarios.hint: Which tenancy-level construct is permanently anchored where the tenancy was born?
scenarios.prompt: What happens?
scenarios.situation: A new tenancy is created with home region us-ashburn-1. Six months later, compliance requires IAM changes to be administered from the EU. The admin tries to 'move' the home region to eu-frankfurt-1.
scenarios.title: The home region lock-in
scenarios.why: The home region is chosen at signup and is immutable: it hosts the tenancy's IAM definitions. You can subscribe to other regions for compute, storage, and networking workloads, but IAM (users, groups, compartments, policies) is anchored to the home region. Choose it deliberately at signup.

choices: A realm is an isolated logical collection of regions (e.g., commercial vs. government realms) with separate identity — workloads cannot span realms, so government work needs a tenancy in the government realm
A realm is a billing construct — all regions in a realm share one invoice
A realm is a synonym for availability domain in older documentation
Realms are optional labels with no isolation effect
scenarios.hint: Think of realms as the highest-level isolation boundary — above even regions.
scenarios.prompt: What is a realm in OCI, and what is the practical implication?
scenarios.situation: A US federal contractor asks whether their OCI tenancy can share identity and network plumbing with their commercial workloads. They heard the phrase 'realm' and want to know if it matters.
scenarios.title: The government cloud question
scenarios.why: Realms partition OCI's global infrastructure into isolated collections of regions — the commercial realm, government realms, and others. Identity, and therefore tenancies, do not cross realm boundaries. A contractor needing government-region services must operate a tenancy inside that realm; they cannot extend a commercial tenancy into it.

choices: Put a CDN/content-delivery layer in front of the bucket (e.g., serve via edge caching) so assets are cached near users; moving the bucket helps but only for one region's users
Archive tier moves data physically closer to requestors, so switch the bucket to Archive
Object Storage is global, so the bucket location is irrelevant — the issue must be DNS
Increase the bucket's storage class to 'Performance' tier
scenarios.hint: The users are global, but the bucket is regional. What sits between them?
scenarios.prompt: What is the more targeted fix, and why?
scenarios.situation: Users in São Paulo report slow page loads for static assets served from an Object Storage bucket in us-ashburn-1. The team proposes moving the bucket to sa-saopaulo-1.
scenarios.title: The latency complaint
scenarios.why: Object Storage buckets live in a specific region; cross-ocean reads add latency. A CDN caches content at edge locations close to users worldwide, which fixes latency for all geographies at once. Moving the bucket only relocates the problem. (There is no 'Performance' tier for Object Storage — Standard and Archive are the tiers.)

choices: Resize to a smaller Flex shape (e.g., 2 OCPUs / 16 GB) — Flex shapes let you pick OCPU and memory independently instead of fixed sizes
Switch to a bare-metal shape — bare metal is always cheaper than VMs
Flex shapes are fixed at 64 OCPUs; the only fix is terminating the tenancy
Move to Dedicated VM Hosts — tenancy-level billing is cheaper
scenarios.hint: What does 'Flex' actually flex?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right compute choice, and what makes Flex shapes useful?
scenarios.situation: A team launches a VM.Standard.E5.Flex instance with 64 OCPUs and 512 GB RAM for a small internal wiki. The bill shocks them. The workload needs about 2 OCPUs.
scenarios.title: The overprovisioned VM
scenarios.why: Flex shapes (VM.Standard.E4/E5/E6.Flex) let you customize the OCPU count and memory, so you pay for what the workload needs. Fixed shapes come in preset sizes; bare metal gives a whole server (no hypervisor) for isolation/noisy-neighbor-sensitive workloads, not for saving money on a wiki.

choices: Preemptible instances — deep discount in exchange for capacity that OCI can reclaim with short notice; fine for checkpointed, resumable batch work
Reserved capacity — cheaper, but it locks the workload to a fixed shape for a year
Burstable instances — same price, better peak performance
Spot markets do not exist in OCI; the only option is on-demand
scenarios.hint: Which pricing option trades a guarantee for a discount?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI option fits, and what is the trade-off?
scenarios.situation: A nightly ETL batch is fault-tolerant, checkpointed, and stateless — it can be interrupted and resumed. The team pays on-demand rates and wants the bill cut without code changes.
scenarios.title: The batch-job discount
scenarios.why: Preemptible instances offer steep discounts because OCI may reclaim the capacity when needed — ideal for interruptible, checkpointed batch/CI workloads. The trade-off is exactly that interruption risk. Reserved capacity is for steady-state committed use; burstable instances handle spiky CPU on small shapes, not bulk discounts.

choices: OCI Functions — serverless, event-triggered, pay-per-execution; no cluster to manage, ideal for sporadic event-driven work
OKE — cheaper because Kubernetes nodes are free
Compute VMs with cron — simplest and most 'cloud native'
Object Storage lifecycle rules can run the thumbnailing natively
scenarios.hint: Which service runs code without you provisioning anything that runs it?
scenarios.prompt: Which fits better, and why?
scenarios.situation: Every image uploaded to an Object Storage bucket must be thumbnailed within seconds, a few hundred times a day, with zero servers to manage. The team debates OKE vs Functions.
scenarios.title: The event-driven thumbnailer
scenarios.why: OCI Functions is the serverless platform: code runs on events (like an Object Storage upload via Events service + Notifications), scales to zero, and bills per execution. OKE (managed Kubernetes) is for container orchestration you manage — overkill for a sporadic thumbnailer. Lifecycle rules manage object retention/tiering, not code execution.

choices: Instance configurations (template of launch parameters + custom image) combined with instance pools for multi-AD rollout and autoscaling
Manual launch 50 times and document the clicks in a runbook
Block volume clones — clone one volume 50 times and boot from each
IAM policies can stamp out identical instances when written per-AD
scenarios.hint: What OCI object is literally a saved 'launch this again' template?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI features automate this repeatably?
scenarios.situation: A team must launch 50 identical web servers across 3 ADs, each from a hardened custom image with the same cloud-init bootstrap. Doing it by hand in the console is error-prone.
scenarios.title: The golden-image rollout
scenarios.why: An instance configuration captures the launch recipe (shape, image, metadata/cloud-init, networking). An instance pool uses it to launch and manage many instances across ADs/fault domains, with autoscaling and rolling updates. Custom images preserve the hardened OS state; cloud-init handles per-boot setup.

choices: OCI Bastion service — managed, time-limited SSH sessions to private instances with no public IPs or standing jump hosts; access is granted per-session and audited
Open SSH (port 22) on the database servers' public IPs with key auth
A NAT gateway — it proxies inbound SSH securely
IAM policies that allow SSH from anywhere
scenarios.hint: Which service gives you SSH to a private instance without the instance — or any jump box — having a public IP?
scenarios.prompt: What is the OCI-native replacement?
scenarios.situation: Engineers SSH to a public jump host, then hop to private-subnet database servers. The jump host is internet-facing with a public IP, and the security team wants that pattern gone.
scenarios.title: The SSH jump-box habit
scenarios.why: Bastion provides just-in-time SSH access to private-subnet resources without public IPs or a persistent bastion host: sessions are time-boxed, authenticated via IAM, and logged. A NAT gateway only allows outbound-initiated traffic (no inbound SSH), and public IPs on databases expand the attack surface.

choices: OS Management Hub — manages packages/errata across fleets, schedules patch jobs, and reports compliance from one place
Cloud Guard — it pushes OS patches as part of threat remediation
Block Volume backups — restoring from backup applies patches
The Events service — it emails when patches are available
scenarios.hint: Which service's whole job is 'which of my 200 servers is missing this erratum'?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI service centralizes this?
scenarios.situation: 200 Oracle Linux instances across three compartments need the same security errata applied on a schedule, with a report of which instances are non-compliant. Today it's ad-hoc SSH loops.
scenarios.title: The patch Tuesday sprawl
scenarios.why: OS Management Hub is the fleet patch-management service for Oracle Linux (and Windows): register instances, define software sources, schedule patch windows, and get compliance reporting. Cloud Guard is a security-posture/threat detector, not a patcher; backups are recovery, not maintenance.

choices: Peered VCNs must have non-overlapping CIDRs — re-create one VCN with a distinct range (e.g., 10.1.0.0/16); plan IP space before peering
VCNs in different regions can never be peered
The CIDR is too large; peering requires /24 or smaller
Peering requires both VCNs to be in the same compartment
scenarios.hint: If two networks both claim 10.0.0.0/16, where does a packet to 10.0.5.7 go?
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A company builds VCN-A (10.0.0.0/16) and VCN-B (10.0.0.0/16) in different regions, then tries to peer them so apps can talk privately. Peering creation fails.
scenarios.title: The overlapping CIDR trap
scenarios.why: VCN peering (local via LPG, or remote via DRG) routes between CIDR blocks — overlapping ranges make routes ambiguous, so OCI requires non-overlapping CIDRs (up to 5 CIDR blocks per VCN including the primary). Remote peering across regions is supported; compartment placement doesn't matter for peering, only IAM.

choices: Network Security Groups — stateful rules applied to a set of VNICs (the app tier), independent of subnet; security lists are subnet-level and stateless
A second VCN — databases must live in their own VCN
Route tables — deny routes are more precise than security rules
Change the database port — security through obscurity is sufficient
scenarios.hint: Which construct is stateful, and which one follows the VNIC instead of the subnet?
scenarios.prompt: What should they use, and what is the key difference from security lists?
scenarios.situation: A database in a private subnet accepts connections from any instance in the VCN because the security list allows 0.0.0.0/0 on port 1521. The team wants only the app tier to reach it, with rules that move with the instances.
scenarios.title: The database that answered everyone
scenarios.why: Security lists attach to subnets and are stateless (return traffic needs explicit egress rules). NSGs attach to VNICs and are stateful (return traffic is automatically allowed), and membership follows the instance, not the subnet. For tier-to-tier filtering (only app servers → DB:1521), NSGs are the precise tool.

choices: NAT gateway — allows outbound-initiated connections to the internet while blocking inbound initiation; an internet gateway requires public IPs and permits inbound
Internet gateway — private subnets can use it as long as route tables are correct
Service gateway — it proxies all internet traffic, not just OCI services
Dynamic Routing Gateway — it NATs outbound traffic automatically
scenarios.hint: Which gateway's entire purpose is 'outbound only'?
scenarios.prompt: Which gateway is correct, and why not an internet gateway?
scenarios.situation: App servers in a private subnet (no public IPs) must download OS patches from the internet, but nothing on the internet may initiate connections to them. The team considers an internet gateway.
scenarios.title: The private subnet that needed updates
scenarios.why: A NAT gateway gives private resources outbound internet access (patch downloads) with no inbound path; instances keep no public IPs. An internet gateway enables two-way traffic and needs public IPs. A service gateway reaches OCI services (Object Storage, etc.) over the private backbone — not the public internet. DRG connects to on-premises/other VCNs.

choices: Dynamic Routing Gateway — attach the VCNs and connect on-premises via Site-to-Site VPN or FastConnect; the DRG routes between them
Internet gateway on each VCN with VPN software on an instance
Local peering gateways chained VCN-to-VCN-to-datacenter
A NAT gateway with static routes to the datacenter
scenarios.hint: Which component is literally called a 'gateway' that routes between VCNs and the corporate network?
scenarios.prompt: What is the OCI hub for this, and which connection types attach to it?
scenarios.situation: A company must connect its datacenter to three OCI VCNs (prod, dev, shared-services) over a private encrypted path, with on-premises routes propagated automatically.
scenarios.title: The on-prem bridge
scenarios.why: The DRG is the regional virtual router: VCNs attach to it, and on-premises networks connect through it via IPSec Site-to-Site VPN (encrypted over internet) or FastConnect (private dedicated circuit). Remote peering between VCNs also goes through the DRG. LPGs peer VCNs but don't reach on-premises.

choices: The subnets use different DNS label configurations or the VCN's DNS label is missing — private DNS resolution of hostnames requires consistent DNS labels; check the VCN/subnet DNS settings
Instances in different subnets can never resolve each other
DNS only works with public IPs in OCI
The instances need an internet gateway for DNS
scenarios.hint: Hostname resolution in OCI depends on what label settings?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
scenarios.situation: Two instances in the same VCN can't resolve each other by hostname. DNS resolution is enabled on the VCN, and the instances are in different subnets.
scenarios.title: The hostname that wouldn't resolve
scenarios.why: OCI's private DNS resolves instance hostnames within a VCN when DNS resolution is enabled and DNS labels are set on the VCN/subnets (instances get FQDNs like host.subnet.vcn.oraclevcn.com). Missing labels or disabled resolution breaks hostname lookup; security rules don't block DNS to the VCN resolver (169.254.169.254). Cross-subnet private DNS works fine.

choices: The load-balancing policy (e.g., round-robin vs. least-connections vs. IP-hash) and session persistence settings — IP-hash or sticky sessions can pin clients to one backend
Add more backend servers — uneven traffic always means under-capacity
The VCN CIDR is too small to balance across
Health check interval — passing checks prove the policy is correct
scenarios.hint: If health checks pass but traffic is lopsided, what decides which backend gets each request?
scenarios.prompt: What should be investigated first?
scenarios.situation: Three web servers sit behind a load balancer, but one server gets most traffic and occasionally times out. Health checks are passing.
scenarios.title: The uneven traffic complaint
scenarios.why: OCI Load Balancer supports policies like weighted round robin, least connections, and IP hash, plus session persistence. IP-hash or sticky sessions concentrate clients on one backend even when all are healthy — that's a policy behavior, not a capacity problem. Verify the policy and persistence config before scaling.

choices: (a) Block Volumes for the database — low-latency block devices; (b) Object Storage Archive tier for backups — cheapest long-term retention, restored when needed
(a) Object Storage for the database — objects are faster than blocks; (b) Block Volumes for backups
(a) File Storage for both — NFS handles databases and backups equally
(a) Boot volumes for the database — boot volumes are optimized for data files
scenarios.hint: Databases need block devices; cold backups need the cheapest byte. Which services are which?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI storage services fit each need?
scenarios.situation: A team needs storage for (a) a database's data files requiring low-latency block access, and (b) 10 TB of immutable nightly backups retained for years, rarely read.
scenarios.title: The backup-target debate
scenarios.why: Block Volumes provide durable, low-latency block storage for databases (attachable/detachable, with backup policies). Object Storage Archive tier is the lowest-cost option for rarely-accessed data with long retention; Standard tier is for hot data. File Storage (NFS) suits shared file workloads, not database data files.

choices: Object versioning — keeps prior versions of an object when overwritten or deleted, so the previous report is recoverable from the version history
Multipart upload — it automatically keeps a copy of each part
Pre-authenticated requests — they snapshot the bucket on each read
Replication — it copies objects to another region instantly
scenarios.hint: Which bucket setting keeps history when an object is replaced?
scenarios.prompt: What Object Storage feature would have saved them, and how does it behave?
scenarios.situation: A monthly financial report in Object Storage was overwritten by a bad upload. The team needs yesterday's version back.
scenarios.title: The overwritten report
scenarios.why: Enabling versioning on a bucket preserves earlier versions whenever an object is overwritten or deleted — you can list and restore the prior version. Replication copies data to another region for DR (doesn't help recover an overwritten object in-place), and PARs grant time-limited access, not history.

choices: A scheduled block-volume backup policy (e.g., daily incremental) assigned to the volume — automated, incremental backups with defined retention
Object Storage lifecycle rules — they back up block volumes automatically
Volume clones — clones are continuous backups
RAID inside the instance — the cloud equivalent of a backup policy
scenarios.hint: Which feature is literally a recurring schedule attached to the volume?
scenarios.prompt: What should have been in place?
scenarios.situation: A corrupted block volume took down production at 2 AM. The last manual snapshot was 3 weeks old. The DBA asks: 'Why wasn't this automatic?'
scenarios.title: The 2 AM page
scenarios.why: OCI backup policies attach to block/boot volumes and run scheduled full + incremental backups to Object Storage with retention rules — the standard automated protection. Clones are point-in-time copies (useful for dev/test), not a backup schedule. Lifecycle rules manage object retention, not volume backups.

choices: File Storage — a managed NFS file system mountable by many instances concurrently
Block Volumes — attach one volume to all 12 instances in read-write mode
Object Storage — mount it as a POSIX filesystem for config files
Boot volumes — share one boot volume across instances
scenarios.hint: Which service speaks NFS to many clients at once?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI service replaces the rsync mesh?
scenarios.situation: Twelve web servers need read/write access to the same configuration directory and shared uploads. Each server currently rsyncs from a primary — drift and conflicts are constant.
scenarios.title: The shared-config problem
scenarios.why: File Storage provides a managed NFSv3 file system that many compute instances mount simultaneously — the native shared-filesystem answer. A block volume attaches to one instance (multi-attach is limited/specialized); Object Storage is an object API, not POSIX file semantics.

choices: Pre-authenticated request — a time-limited URL granting upload access to the bucket/prefix without an IAM identity
Make the bucket public for 30 days, then private again
Share the tenancy admin credentials with an expiry note
Object Storage lifecycle rules grant temporary write access
scenarios.hint: Which feature is a signed, expiring URL for a bucket?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right mechanism?
scenarios.situation: An external partner must upload weekly CSVs into a private Object Storage bucket for 30 days. The team must not create an IAM user for them.
scenarios.title: The partner upload link
scenarios.why: Pre-authenticated requests (PARs) grant scoped, expiring access to a bucket or object prefix via URL — no IAM user needed. They can allow writes (uploads) as well as reads, and expire automatically. Public buckets and shared credentials are never the answer.

choices: Data Transfer service (offline disk shipment) — copy to encrypted transfer disks/devices, ship to Oracle, data is uploaded to Object Storage
Keep the 100 Mbps upload running and throttle it to business hours
Compress the archives — compression ratios guarantee it fits in a week
FastConnect — it increases the existing internet uplink speed
scenarios.hint: When the network is the bottleneck and the data is huge, what moves instead of packets?
scenarios.prompt: What is the practical OCI option?
scenarios.situation: A datacenter with a 100 Mbps uplink must move 40 TB of archives into OCI Object Storage. At current speed the transfer takes over a month, and the uplink is saturated.
scenarios.title: The 40 TB migration
scenarios.why: For bulk offline ingest, OCI's Data Transfer service ships encrypted disks (or the Transfer Appliance for petabytes) to Oracle for direct upload — far faster than a thin uplink for 40 TB. FastConnect is a private network circuit (great for steady hybrid traffic, not a magic uplink upgrade), and compression can't be assumed to fix a 37-day transfer.

choices: Design a compartment hierarchy (e.g., by environment/team) and scope policies to the least-privilege compartment — compartments are the primary isolation and policy boundary
Create more admin users so no single key is critical
Move everything to a new tenancy — compartments can't be added later
Disable IAM — it adds complexity without security benefit
scenarios.hint: What is the unit that both organizes resources and scopes policies?
scenarios.prompt: What is the foundational IAM remediation?
scenarios.situation: Everything — prod, dev, finance data — lives in the root compartment with broad admin policies. An intern's compromised key touched production.
scenarios.title: The flat-tenancy mess
scenarios.why: Compartments are OCI's fundamental organizing and isolation unit: policies grant group permissions on specific compartments, so a compromised credential scoped to dev can't reach prod. Design the hierarchy (up to 6 levels deep, including root) around blast-radius boundaries, then write least-privilege policies per compartment.

choices: Dynamic group — define the instance(s) by OCID/compartment, then write a policy granting that dynamic group access to Vault secrets and the bucket; no static credentials
Embed the API key and rotate it monthly via cron
Give the instance the tenancy admin's key — simplest
Secrets can't be read from instances; copy them at deploy time
scenarios.hint: How can an instance itself be the 'who' in a policy, with no password involved?
scenarios.prompt: What is the secure pattern, and how is it authorized?
scenarios.situation: An app on a compute instance must read secrets from Vault and write to a specific bucket. The team is tempted to bake an IAM user's API key into the image.
scenarios.title: The instance that needed a secret
scenarios.why: Dynamic groups let OCI resources (instances, functions) act as principals: matching rules select them, and policies grant the dynamic group permissions — the instance authenticates with its own identity via instance principals, no stored keys. Baking user keys into images leaks credentials to anyone with the image.

choices: Oracle secures the cloud (physical, hypervisor, network fabric); the customer secures what's IN the cloud — data, IAM policies, OS patching, security lists
Oracle handles everything above the hypervisor, including customer IAM policies
The customer handles physical datacenter security in OCI
Responsibility is split 50/50 on every control
scenarios.hint: Who configures the bucket policy — Oracle or you?
scenarios.prompt: Where does the shared responsibility line fall for IaaS?
scenarios.situation: After a misconfigured bucket leaks data, the customer tells auditors 'security is Oracle's job in the cloud.'
scenarios.title: The 'Oracle handles it' myth
scenarios.why: The shared model: Oracle owns security OF the cloud (facilities, hardware, virtualization, physical network); the customer owns security IN the cloud — their data classification, IAM least privilege, guest OS patching, firewall rules, and encryption choices. A public bucket is squarely customer-side.

choices: Cloud Guard — continuously monitors for misconfigurations and risky activity, flags problems, and can auto-remediate with responder rules
Vault — it detects misconfigurations as a side effect of key storage
Cloud Advisor — it only optimizes cost, not security
Audit logs alone — reading them daily is the intended workflow
scenarios.hint: Which service watches your tenancy and says 'that bucket shouldn't be public'?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI service fits?
scenarios.situation: Over months, buckets become public, ports open to 0.0.0.0/0, and keys go unrotated. The team wants continuous detection of these misconfigurations with guided remediation.
scenarios.title: The drifting configuration
scenarios.why: Cloud Guard is OCI's security-posture management: detector rules spot issues (public buckets, open security lists, etc.), and responder rules can fix them automatically. Audit service records API activity (the evidence trail); Vault stores keys/secrets. Detection + guided response is Cloud Guard's job.

choices: OCI Vault (Key Management) — create customer-managed keys, control rotation, and assign them to volumes/buckets; Oracle-managed keys are the default otherwise
Cloud Guard — it generates encryption keys during scans
IAM policies — they encrypt data at rest when written correctly
Object Storage versioning — versions are encrypted with separate keys
scenarios.hint: Which service is the key-management system, not the policy system?
scenarios.prompt: What provides this in OCI?
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires customer-managed encryption keys for block volumes and buckets, with key rotation and no Oracle access to key material.
scenarios.title: The encryption-key question
scenarios.why: OCI encrypts data at rest by default with Oracle-managed keys. Vault (KMS) lets you create and control your own master keys — including keys backed by HSMs — and bind them to block volumes, boot volumes, and buckets, with rotation policies. IAM authorizes; it doesn't encrypt.

choices: OCI WAF for Layer-7 filtering (bot management, OWASP rules) in front of the app; OCI's edge/DDoS protection absorbs volumetric network-layer attacks
Security lists — they inspect HTTP payloads
NAT gateway — it filters inbound attack traffic
Bastion — it proxies web traffic securely
scenarios.hint: Which service understands HTTP requests, not just packets?
scenarios.prompt: Which OCI services address the network and application layers?
scenarios.situation: A public web app behind a load balancer is hit by an HTTP flood and credential-stuffing attempts. The load balancer distributes the attack evenly to all backends.
scenarios.title: The Layer-7 flood
scenarios.why: WAF inspects HTTP/S traffic against managed rules (OWASP Top 10, bots, rate limiting) before it reaches the load balancer. Network-layer DDoS absorption happens at OCI's edge. Security lists are L3/L4 packet filters (no payload inspection); NAT gateways only do outbound.

choices: Budgets with alert rules (email/notifications at thresholds) plus Cost Analysis tracking by compartment/tag — detect spend early, attribute it precisely
Delete the tenancy monthly and recreate it — guarantees zero carryover spend
Budgets hard-stop resources when exceeded — set a $0 budget
Invoices are the only cost signal OCI provides
scenarios.hint: Which two tools give you 'warn me at 80%' and 'who spent it'?
scenarios.prompt: What OCI cost-control combo prevents the next surprise?
scenarios.situation: A dev team's experiment left GPU instances running for three weeks. Finance saw it on the invoice — a month later.
scenarios.title: The surprise invoice
scenarios.why: Budgets track spend/forecast against thresholds and fire alerts (via Notifications) — they alert, they don't auto-terminate. Cost Analysis with compartment/tag grouping attributes spend to teams. Tagging resources (cost-tracking tags) is what makes the attribution work; quotas can actually cap resource counts.

choices: Quotas — set compartment-level limits on resource counts (e.g., max instances); autoscaling cannot exceed them
Budgets — they terminate instances over budget
IAM policies — they limit CPU counts directly
Cost Analysis — it rolls back excess resources
scenarios.hint: Which control says 'this compartment may never contain more than N instances'?
scenarios.prompt: What governance control caps resource creation regardless of autoscaling?
scenarios.situation: An autoscaling pool in dev has no upper bound configured in policy; a bug loops scale-out and the compartment hits the tenancy's shape limits — then the request goes to support for a limit increase, which would make it worse.
scenarios.title: The runaway autoscale
scenarios.why: Quotas enforce hard ceilings on how many of each resource type a compartment may contain — the backstop against runaway automation. Budgets only alert on spend. IAM policies authorize actions, not quantities. Combine quotas (quantity guardrail) with budgets (spend signal).

choices: Pay-as-you-go bills metered usage with no commitment; Universal Credits (monthly flex) commit to a spend level for discounted rates across eligible services — steady production fits commitment, spiky dev fits PAYG
Committed credits are only for government customers
PAYG is always cheaper regardless of usage pattern
OCI has a single pricing model; the choice is cosmetic
scenarios.hint: Which model rewards you for promising to spend?
scenarios.prompt: How do the OCI pricing models compare?
scenarios.situation: A company with steady, predictable production workloads plus spiky dev/test asks: pay-as-you-go versus committed credits?
scenarios.title: The pricing-model choice
scenarios.why: PAYG = no commitment, metered billing, maximum flexibility. Universal Credits = commit to an amount (monthly flex or annual) for lower rates, usable across many services — the discount rewards predictable spend. Match steady-state production to commitment and variable dev/test to PAYG.

choices: Always Free includes limited compute (Ampere/micro VMs), Autonomous Database instances, storage, and more — but verify current limits/regions; exceeding them bills at PAYG rates
Always Free covers unlimited usage of every service for students
Always Free requires a paid support plan
Free tier resources can't run databases
scenarios.hint: Free within limits — what happens past the limits?
scenarios.prompt: What does Always Free offer, and what is the catch to verify?
scenarios.situation: A student wants to prototype on OCI for a semester project with zero budget: a small VM, an Oracle database, and some object storage.
scenarios.title: The free-tier prototype
scenarios.why: OCI Always Free provides a set of resources (compute VMs, Autonomous Databases, block/object storage, load balancer, etc.) free for the tenancy's life within published limits. The discipline: know the limits (e.g., VM counts/shapes, storage GB) because overages bill at PAYG — and check the current published terms, which Oracle can change.

choices: Defined (tag-namespace) cost-tracking tags applied at creation, enforced by policy/IAM, grouped in Cost Analysis — freeform tags work but defined tags are governable
Rename all resources with project prefixes — names are the cost signal
Compartments alone are enough; tags add nothing
Budgets automatically infer project ownership
scenarios.hint: Which metadata, applied to resources, does Cost Analysis group by?
scenarios.prompt: What tagging discipline fixes attribution?
scenarios.situation: Finance sees a 40% cost jump but can't tell which project caused it — resources have no consistent labels, and several teams share compartments.
scenarios.title: The mystery spend
scenarios.why: Cost-tracking tags let Cost Analysis slice spend by project/team/owner. Defined tags (under a tag namespace) can be restricted by IAM so only finance's namespace values are used — preventing tag sprawl. Require tags at creation (via policy or process) or attribution stays guesswork.

choices: Higher support tiers offer faster response SLAs and more channels — but choose the tier before the incident; know your current SLA and escalation path now
All tiers have identical 15-minute response for any severity
Support tiers only differ in documentation access
Upgrading mid-incident retroactively speeds up the current ticket
scenarios.hint: When is the right time to learn your support SLA — during the outage or before?
scenarios.prompt: What should they know about OCI support tiers?
scenarios.situation: Production is down at 3 AM. The team has basic OCI support and wonders whether they can get a faster response by 'upgrading mid-incident'.
scenarios.title: The 3 AM severity-1
scenarios.why: OCI support comes in tiers with different response-time targets, channels, and features (e.g., basic vs. paid tiers with faster Sev-1 response). The operational lesson: know your tier's SLA and escalation procedure before you need it; you can't negotiate response times during an outage.
